questions.prompt: What does a tree rotation preserve?

options.text: The in-order (sorted) ordering of the keys
The exact height of every node

questions.explanation: A rotation restructures shape to rebalance while keeping the in-order sequence unchanged — that is why it is a valid BST operation.

questions.prompt: What height do self-balancing BSTs (AVL, red-black) guarantee?
questions.explanation: Balancing keeps the height logarithmic, so search, insert, and delete are guaranteed O(log n) regardless of insertion order.

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: AVL trees are more strictly balanced than red-black trees
Red-black trees typically need fewer rotations per update
Both guarantee O(log n) search, insert, and delete
A plain BST guarantees O(log n) operations without balancing

questions.explanation: AVL is tighter (faster lookups); red-black is looser (fewer rotations, faster updates); both are O(log n). A plain BST does NOT self-balance.

questions.prompt: The O(1) local restructuring that rebalances a BST while preserving key order is called a ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: Rotations rearrange a few nodes to reduce height without changing the in-order sequence.

questions.prompt: Order the steps an AVL tree takes on insertion.

items.text: Insert the key as in an ordinary BST
Update heights along the path back to the root
Compute the balance factor at each node
Rotate to rebalance any node that is out of balance

questions.explanation: AVL insertion first places the key, then walks back up updating heights, checking balance factors, and rotating where needed.

questions.prompt: Match each item with its description.

pairs.right: Color rules; fewer rotations per update

questions.explanation: AVL enforces tight height balance; red-black uses colors for looser balance; rotations do the rebalancing; without balancing a BST can be linear.
